## How it works

- [statement] Preserve each participant’s sequence and context when analyzing entries. Examine how experiences change over time and what circumstances accompany changes; repeated observations support within-person questions as well as comparisons between participants. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/diary-studies/ · keywords: Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling · also: https://www.apa.org/research-practice/conduct-research/sampling-longitudinal-research, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11079761/
- [statement] Distinguish adherence to individual prompts from retention of participants. Missing responses can occur when responding is inconvenient or unsafe, and selective reporting can bias the contexts represented. Longitudinal UX studies should plan for participant dropout as well as incomplete entries. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6925392/ · keywords: Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling · also: https://www.nngroup.com/articles/diary-studies/
- [statement] Signal-contingent capture prompts participants to report when notified. Random or stratified-random signals can sample different moments across the day; choose timing around relevant contexts and participants’ schedules. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/diary-studies/ · keywords: Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling · also: https://www.apa.org/research-practice/conduct-research/sampling-longitudinal-research
- [statement] Onboard participants with plain instructions about what and when to report, the expected detail, tools, and incentives. Explain the importance of timely responses and train participants to recognize the target event or construct. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/diary-studies/ · keywords: Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling · also: https://www.apa.org/research-practice/conduct-research/sampling-longitudinal-research
- [statement] Observational experience sampling can examine co-occurrence, lagged associations, and temporal ordering, but these patterns alone do not establish causation because confounding is not experimentally controlled. (low confidence) — https://m-path.io/learn/what-is-esm/ · keywords: Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling
- [statement] The caregiver EMA study could not isolate the effects of survey length or delivery frequency because participants received the same surveys. Its low-burden findings should not be treated as experimental proof of an optimal protocol. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11079761/ · keywords: Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling

## How-to and procedures

- [statement] Use event-contingent capture for a clearly defined event of interest. It suits infrequent or unpredictable events, but logging every occurrence becomes burdensome when events are frequent. Give participants an unambiguous event definition. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/diary-studies/ · keywords: Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling · also: https://www.apa.org/research-practice/conduct-research/sampling-longitudinal-research
- [statement] Use interval-based capture at predetermined times when periodic reporting fits the question. Check whether the selected times miss intervening events or systematically underrepresent other parts of the day. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/diary-studies/ · keywords: Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling · also: https://www.apa.org/research-practice/conduct-research/sampling-longitudinal-research
- [statement] Use signal-triggered capture when participants should respond to notifications. Signals may follow random or mixed schedules; they can sample different times of day and reduce reliance on participants remembering to initiate entries. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/diary-studies/ · keywords: Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling · also: https://www.apa.org/research-practice/conduct-research/sampling-longitudinal-research
- [statement] Use interval-contingent capture at predetermined times when regular reporting fits the question. Intervals that are too long can miss intervening events; intervals that are too short increase burden. A fixed reporting time can also skew which daily experiences receive detail. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/diary-studies/ · keywords: Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling · also: https://www.apa.org/research-practice/conduct-research/sampling-longitudinal-research

## Problems, failure modes and limitations

- [statement] Keep repeated prompts short and plainly worded. Explain why timely responses matter and train participants to recognize qualifying events when the task cannot be simplified. (medium confidence) — https://www.apa.org/research-practice/conduct-research/sampling-longitudinal-research · keywords: Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling · also: https://www.rallyuxr.com/post/diary-studies-101-an-actionable-guide-for-ux-researchers
- [statement] Repeated measurement can change responses or experiences. APA identifies anticipation of fixed reports as a reactivity risk; Eisele and colleagues found changes in completion time and within-person variability in a student study, while the implications for data validity remained unresolved. (medium confidence) — https://www.apa.org/research-practice/conduct-research/sampling-longitudinal-research · keywords: Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling · also: https://ppw.kuleuven.be/okp/_pdf/Eisele2023AMMII.pdf
- [statement] The severe-mental-disorder ESM meta-analysis found lower compliance with more evaluations per day and shorter spacing, but no significant association with study duration. These associations are population- and reporting-dependent, so they do not establish a universal UX cadence or prove that every longer study causes more attrition. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6925392/ · keywords: Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling

## Comparisons and alternatives

- [statement] UX diary studies collect participants’ self-reported experiences over time in everyday contexts; experience sampling uses repeated momentary reports to examine within-person processes. These reports are sampled accounts rather than a complete behavioral record. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/diary-studies/ · keywords: Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling · also: https://m-path.io/learn/what-is-esm/, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6925392/
- [statement] Fixed schedules can make participation easier to plan but may change the situations participants report from. The ESM meta-analysis did not establish a universally optimal fixed-versus-random schedule and recommends choosing according to the scientific question. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6925392/ · keywords: Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling
- [statement] For temporal analysis, inspect observation gaps instead of treating every missing report as interchangeable: the caregiver EMA paper notes that nonadherence may be nonrandom and connected to the momentary exposures under study, which can impair across-day relationship analyses. (medium confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11079761/ · keywords: Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling · also: https://m-path.io/learn/what-is-esm/
- [statement] Set diary-study duration from the research question, behavior frequency, and the time needed for the activity to unfold; NN/g presents different reporting periods for different behaviors rather than one universal duration. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/diary-studies/ · keywords: Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling
- [statement] Distinguish response compliance from participant retention. In the severe-mental-disorder ESM meta-analysis, compliance measures completed versus protocol-possible evaluations, whereas retention measures participants included in final analyses; minimum-compliance exclusions can link the two. Report definitions and exclusion rules. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6925392/ · keywords: Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling

## Facts and statements

- [statement] Choose duration from the research question, event frequency, and time needed for the activity to unfold. Choose cadence to capture the contexts and temporal changes of interest while limiting reporting burden; a standard number of diary days is not a substitute for this rationale. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/diary-studies/ · keywords: Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling · also: https://www.apa.org/research-practice/conduct-research/sampling-longitudinal-research
- [statement] Prepare clear instructions, expected reporting effort, example entries, and a contact channel. Brief participants on unfamiliar tasks or tools. Pilot the design and materials before the main study, and avoid examples that steer participants toward particular experiences. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/diary-studies/ · keywords: Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling · also: https://medium.com/somiacx/lessons-from-running-a-diary-study-e35ddd1e4060, https://www.rallyuxr.com/post/diary-studies-101-an-actionable-guide-for-ux-researchers
- [statement] High-frequency reports can reduce retrospective recall demands and reveal within-person changes, but scheduled reporting can itself influence responses. Anticipating a fixed reporting time is a possible source of reactivity. (medium confidence) — https://www.apa.org/research-practice/conduct-research/sampling-longitudinal-research · keywords: Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling · also: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6925392/
- [statement] Monitor entries during collection and ask for clarification while the event is fresh. Use a post-study interview to probe ambiguous entries and reflect on the broader experience; diary screenshots or entries can serve as personalized interview prompts. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/diary-studies/ · keywords: Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling · also: https://medium.com/somiacx/lessons-from-running-a-diary-study-e35ddd1e4060
- [statement] In a meta-analysis of ESM studies concerning severe mental disorders, lower sampling frequency and longer intervals were associated with higher compliance. Study duration was not significantly associated with compliance or retention. These are population- and protocol-specific associations, not universal UX cadence thresholds. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6925392/ · keywords: Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling
- [statement] A caregiver EMA study found that momentary experiences and participant characteristics mattered for burden and adherence; its reported burden was low and it found no strong indicators that design attributes created persistent burden. Low adherence should therefore not automatically be interpreted as proof that a protocol is too demanding. (low confidence) — https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11079761/ · keywords: Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling
- [statement] Pilot the protocol before the main study to test instructions, tools, survey length, prompt timing, and burden in everyday contexts; use participant feedback to revise the design. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/diary-studies/ · keywords: Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling · also: https://m-path.io/learn/what-is-esm/
- [statement] NN/g recommends monitoring entries during collection, asking timely clarification questions, and agreeing on a contact method and periodic reminders that do not become overly intrusive. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/diary-studies/ · keywords: Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling
- [statement] Plan a post-study interview grounded in each participant’s entries to clarify vague accounts, probe missing detail, and invite reflection on the broader experience. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/diary-studies/ · keywords: Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling
- [statement] Keep repeated surveys brief and consider participants’ daily routines. Frequent prompts can intrude on activities, and participant burden can affect both response rates and the quality of completed answers. (medium confidence) — https://www.apa.org/research-practice/conduct-research/sampling-longitudinal-research · keywords: Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling · also: https://m-path.io/learn/what-is-esm/
- [statement] Eisele and colleagues caution that their student-sample findings may not generalize to other populations. Behavioral changes were rare, effects of protocol and individual characteristics were inconsistent, and the study did not establish whether observed reactive changes damaged validity. (low confidence) — https://ppw.kuleuven.be/okp/_pdf/Eisele2023AMMII.pdf · keywords: Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling
- [statement] Analyze diary experiences in their temporal and contextual sequence. For quantitative experience-sampling data, account for repeated observations nested within people and temporal dependence; distinguish within-person associations from between-person differences. (medium confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/diary-studies/ · keywords: Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling · also: https://m-path.io/learn/what-is-esm/
- [statement] NN/g warns that incentive rules can distort diary data: response requirements should be realistic, and open-ended payment for extra entries can encourage manufactured interactions. Design compensation around the expected effort and natural activity. (low confidence) — https://www.nngroup.com/articles/diary-studies/ · keywords: Longitudinal UX diary studies and experience sampling
